501.quote_or_event: “He who does not speak untruth from anger or for fun, from greed or from fear, him we call a Brâhmana.”
501.explanation: In the sermon of the monk Jayaghosha, the true Brahmana is the one whose truthfulness holds under every pressure: anger, amusement, greed and fear.
501.tie_back: Valluvar tests a candidate through virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear of death; the Jain verse likewise defines worth as integrity that does not give way to greed, pleasure-seeking or fear.
501.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
501._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The list of pressures (greed, fun, fear) closely parallels the Kural's tests, but the verse describes an ideal monk, not a procedure for testing an appointee.

502.quote_or_event: “hence none is either high or low. After knowing this, who will feel proud of taking birth in respectable or high family?”
502.explanation: Because every soul has been born many times into high and low families, Jainism holds that family rank confers no real distinction; worth lies in conduct.
502.tie_back: The kural looks first to good family as a ground for confidence; the Jain teaching sets family lineage aside and would rest confidence on the faultlessness and moral shame the kural also names.
502.source: Saman Suttam v. 90 (Precepts on Religion, uttama-mardava; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
502._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam (quoted from mid-verse). This is a partial contrast rather than a match: Jainism discounts the lineage criterion the kural leads with.

503.quote_or_event: “You do not know what is most essential in the Vêdas, nor in sacrifices, nor in the heavenly bodies, nor in duties.”
503.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a priest renowned for his Vedic learning that, for all his study, he has missed what is most essential.
503.tie_back: The kural warns that even the deeply learned turn out, on close examination, to have some ignorance; here a famously learned man is examined and found lacking in the essential point.
503.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
503._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good thematic parallel, but the verse is polemical against Brahmanical learning rather than a general remark that no one is free of ignorance (the Jain view that only a kevalin is omniscient is implied, not stated).

504.quote_or_event: Jain epistemology teaches that a thing is known through valid knowledge (pramana) and through partial standpoints (nayas), so that any single viewpoint captures only one aspect of a many-sided reality (anekantavada).
504.explanation: Because reality is many-sided, Jain thinkers insist that judgment weigh several aspects together rather than fix on one feature alone.
504.tie_back: Valluvar asks the examiner to look at a man's virtues and then his faults and judge by what prevails; the Jain doctrine of standpoints similarly warns against a verdict drawn from one side only.
504.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6 (pramana and naya), with the anekantavada doctrine as generally expounded
504._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known doctrine, not verified against Tatia's translation in this session. It is a next-best match: anekantavada concerns knowing reality, not weighing a candidate's merits against faults.

505.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
505.explanation: Jayaghosha teaches that a person's standing is made by deeds, not by birth or outward marks.
505.tie_back: The kural makes each person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness or meanness; the Jain verse likewise makes actions alone the measure of what a person is.
505.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
505._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close in substance; the touchstone image itself is absent, though 25.21 nearby compares the true Brahmana to gold purified in fire.

506.quote_or_event: “He who has given up his former connections (with his parents, &c.), with his kinsmen and relations, and who is not given to pleasure, him we call a Brâhmana.”
506.explanation: For the Jain monastic ideal, cutting ties with kin is a mark of spiritual worth rather than of untrustworthiness.
506.tie_back: The kural distrusts those without kin because they have nothing binding them to shame; Jainism honours the monk who has deliberately given up kin, an honest contrast in values, though it presumes he is bound instead by his vows.
506.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
506._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Offered as a contrast: the verse values the renunciation of kin that the kural treats as a warning sign for worldly office.

507.quote_or_event: “But he who puts bad bullocks before his car, will be tired out with beating them; he will feel vexation, and his goad will be broken (at last).”
507.explanation: The teacher Garga compares unfit pupils to bad bullocks yoked to a cart: whoever harnesses them reaps only exhaustion and frustration.
507.tie_back: The kural says trusting the unfit out of fondness brings every folly; Garga's image shows the same result of yoking unfit helpers to one's work.
507.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
507._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong on the consequence of using unfit people, but the kural's specific fault, choosing out of affection, is not named.

508.quote_or_event: “Just as a person is free while climbing a tree but once he starts falling then he has no power to check it.”
508.explanation: The Jain teaching on karma says a person is free when binding karma but loses control once its consequences begin to unfold.
508.tie_back: The kural warns that a careless act of trust lets loose sorrow that cannot be recalled; the Jain image makes the same point that the choice is free but its fall cannot be stopped.
508.source: Saman Suttam v. 60 (Precepts on Karma; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
508._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com (first sentence of the verse only). It is a general karmic analogy, and Jain doctrine holds karma to be individual, so the kural's sorrow passing to descendants has no counterpart.

509.quote_or_event: The Jain teacher Haribhadra is remembered for declaring that he had no partiality for Mahavira and no hatred for Kapila, and that whoever's words are reasonable should be accepted.
509.explanation: Haribhadra insisted that even religious trust must follow rational examination rather than prior loyalty.
509.tie_back: The kural says trust no one without examination and, once examined, trust fittingly; Haribhadra applies the same order of examining first and then trusting to the teachers one follows.
509.source: Haribhadra, Lokatattvanirnaya (famous couplet; attribution as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Haribhadra')
509._accuracy_note: Paraphrased only; the verse's wording circulates in variants and was not checked against a primary edition, so attribution rests on a secondary web source. Good fit on 'examine before trusting', applied to doctrine rather than people.

510.quote_or_event: “The persons possessed of Right Faith are free from doubts and are therefore fearless.”
510.explanation: Freedom from doubt (nihshankita) is the first of the eight limbs of right faith: once the truth has been tested and accepted, wavering suspicion is a fault.
510.tie_back: The kural condemns doubting one already examined and trusted; Jainism likewise counts doubt about what has been rightly accepted as a flaw that brings fear and instability.
510.source: Saman Suttam v. 232 (Essential requisites of Right Faith; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
510._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com (first sentence of the verse). The parallel is structural; the Jain verse concerns doubt about religious truth, not distrust of a vetted person, and it does not address the first error (trusting without examination).
